AI
Nvidia
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
by
Kat Tenbarge
Nov 24, 2026, 4:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge; Getty Images
Tech
AI
Nvidia
Jensen Huang deepfakes are the hot new AI slop
Influencers are chasing viral success with the saga — and tech stack — of Nvidia’s CEO.
by
Kat Tenbarge
Nov 24, 2026, 4:30 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Kat Tenbarge
is the author of
Spitfire News,
a newsletter about internet culture, politics, and media.
Jensen Huang is partying it up in Ibiza. In
a video
with nearly 6 million views on Instagram, the former CEO of Nvidia is dancing in a crowded club, champagne glass in hand, still wearing his signature black leather jacket. Suddenly, from behind him, Alice Huang — the Chinese technology executive and suspected spy he
had an affair with
, sparking congressional investigations and his resignation from the chipmaking company he cofounded — appears. She puts her hand on his shoulder and he wraps his arm around her waist as they begin dancing together. The video’s caption reads “Honey Trap Final Boss. #inthemoodforlove.”
Of course, it’s AI-generated. This Instagram Reel is one of hundreds of AI deepfakes featuring Huang, his wife Lori, Alice, and sometimes Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell (the second of three
reported affair partners
). In this case, Huang is being swapped into an existing meme called “
Ibiza Final Boss
.” The original video featured a British construction worker with a bowl cut dancing in exactly the same way, minus a woman sidling up to him. Other viral AI hits include Huang
in a scene
from
The Office
, Huang in the
music video
for George Michael’s “Careless Whisper,” and Huang as
the former Astronomer CEO
who got
caught in an affair
with one of his employees by the jumbotron at a Coldplay concert last summer. Even the rapper 50 Cent
posted
an AI edit of his “P.I.M.P.” music video, now featuring Huang with some flashy silver accessories.
Unlike deepfake pornography or election disinformation, these AI videos aren’t necessarily intended to harm or mislead people. They’re memes making fun of Huang’s cheating scandal and its global implications, created with AI technology that in many cases relies heavily on Nvidia’s tech stack: video diffusion models running on the Nvidia GPUs that power much of the modern generative AI industry. “It’s ironic that without Nvidia generating millions of these AI memes ... would not be possible,” reads one of the top comments on the Ibiza deepfake. “In some sense, Jensen is making Nvidia richer by his own scandal.” The comment was punctuated by multiple cry-laughing emoji.
As it turns out, Huang may benefit, too. On Monday, the Nvidia board
announced
he was reinstated as president, CEO, and board director following “a series of discussions and meetings” and “input from senior levels of the United States government.” Nvidia’s stock has
since surged
, and new AI Huang memes cast him in a victorious light.
One variation
swaps him into a scene from
The Wolf of Wall Street
, announcing “I’m not leaving” to a crowd of cheering men that has been edited to include AI versions of Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg.
Related
Welcome to elite impunity, Jensen Huang
Trump engineered a risky comeback for Jensen Huang
While the saga continues, many social media users are finding the humor in these Huang deepfakes, and their creators are churning out variations to meet the sudden demand. The Instagram account behind the Ibiza one has made three Huang deepfakes so far, all remakes of the same scene.
Another version
features Powell dancing with him, and the
third one
shows a sea of young women in bikini tops and shorts surrounding Huang, who lifts his champagne up in celebration. Each has accrued millions of views.
“His story has just come at the best time for ai creators and a terrible time for him,” wrote the account behind the Ibiza videos in a direct message to
The Verge
. “Everyone was doing him. Most I’ve seen anyone AI-ed.”
This deepfake creator identified himself as a 40-year-old man from Melbourne, Australia, but wouldn’t share his real name. He says he has spent “thousands” on AI video generation, using models like TikTok developer ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 and Alibaba’s Wan 3. These, along with other AI tools like Google’s Nano Banana, help power the ecosystem of deepfakes.
He said his Instagram page has been going “super viral” in the past two weeks, thanks to the Ibiza meme format. He has nearly 100 million views on various iterations of it featuring different celebrities. The Huang ones are among the most popular, alongside versions featuring
Elizabeth Holmes
and
Amanda Seyfried
playing her in the hit Nathan Fielder documentary
You Can See Everything
.
“I wanted to elevate the content and know that putting what is happening in the news ... would get traction,” he wrote. “Always wanted to be a filmmaker but this technology is beyond whatever I imagined was possible.”
As generative AI has taken hold of the internet in recent years, a lot of the resulting viral content has been disparaged as “
AI slop
.”
Hollywood productions
,
mainstream artists
, and even
local businesses
have been maligned for using (or appearing to use) AI in their advertisements and final cuts. Video trends like putting
sexy AI fruit characters
in
Love Island
parodies racked up millions of views online but failed to deliver any real cultural momentum. The ubiquity of the Huang deepfakes and the relative lack of blowback from AI critics may indicate that the future of AI-generated content is similar to the rest of meme culture: If the topic’s trending, people will engage with something, even if it’s following the same formula as the slop. That an AI tech titan’s own indiscretions are inspiring this latest evolution in deepfakes is just the sardonic cherry on top.
“It’s not that we’re inundated in deepfakes of Trump being like ‘Nuclear war tomorrow,’ like the way it was framed as the big problem,” says misinformation researcher Abbie Richards. “Instead, it just feels like there is so much slop to push through to have any grounding in reality.”
The AI memes of Huang and other public figures don’t feel as sinister as other forms of AI disinformation and misinformation, mainly because of how goofy they are. It’s hard to imagine anyone falling for a “
Gangnam Style
” parody or any serious implications if they did. But these deepfakes are still eerily realistic, as one comment on the Seyfried Ibiza variation pointed out: “All jokes aside, is anyone else finding it increasingly alarming that AI is capable of this?”
Even the creator behind the Ibiza AI videos thinks “someone will try and clamp down because it’s getting outta control.” But in the meantime, he’s looking for ways to monetize his newfound virality. Despite his significant financial outlay, he says he hasn’t made any money yet, besides getting “gifted $3 on a reel once.”
While Instagram has started to invite some creators to earn direct payouts from views on their Reels, the account behind the AI “Careless Whisper” parody featuring Huang told
The Verge
that “the way to earn is through creating content for clients and companies after gaining attention on social media.” This AI creator, who declined to share any identifying information, wrote in a direct message that they receive dozens of requests from new and returning clients for AI commissions every time they go viral, “which is quite often.” In addition to Huang deepfakes, some of their most viral AI edits feature Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man
as a rapper
.
The Ibiza AI meme creator has worked with one celebrity brand so far, belonging to the Irish mixed martial artist Conor McGregor. Four months ago, McGregor launched an energy drink called MAC Energy, and the company requested an AI Ibiza meme showing McGregor dancing with a can of it. The creator complied, and
the post
exists as a collaboration between the two Instagram pages, but it isn’t labeled as an advertisement and he says he didn’t ask for any money in return.
“I just did it because it was a good opportunity for my page,” he says.
It seems like the entity that stands to reap the biggest reward from viral Huang deepfakes is Instagram itself and the other social media sites where creators are posting them. And these humorous AI edits are technically allowed on Meta platforms,
as long as
creators disclose that they’re AI-generated. Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment by publication time.
But there are other considerations besides profitability. Many of these AI memes hinge on sexist portrayals and racist stereotypes as the joke. Asian American women in Silicon Valley have reported an
uptick in microaggressions
revolving around “honeypot” and “Chinese spy” allegations. And when it comes to Powell and the other Nvidia employee who Huang reportedly had a relationship with, the workplace power dynamic at play has faded into the background of mockery.
The more troubling dynamics of Huang’s affairs have faded into the background of mockery
“Even though we know that he was wielding his power to have inappropriate relationships with his subordinates and his employees, it’s still like ‘LOL, let’s make an AI deepfake of him at the office,’” says Josh Lora, a writer and creator who has a
popular TikTok series
about the role of cheating scandals in American culture. “Why aren’t we having a real conversation about the effects of this on women, the effects of this workplace on women, especially 10 years after #MeToo?”
The apparent lack of interest from major social media companies to stem the flow of this kind of disparaging AI content isn’t surprising to misinformation expert Richards, even as some
tech CEOs
, like Elon Musk, called for Huang’s reinstatement and cast doubt on the reporting against him. If Huang memes are truly in vogue, that may be worth more to the AI industry than his dignity.
“I think that they are invested in the widespread adoption of AI,” she says. “So anything with AI going viral and appearing to be popular and liked by the public probably, in their mind, benefits them.”
With Huang back as CEO, the message couldn’t be clearer: For him, the consequences of his affairs were temporary, including whatever humiliation stemmed from the AI memes. Ultimately, all any of it meant was more power for Nvidia and more power for Jensen
Huang.

The Verge
and
posted on Threads
, two of the
Times
’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
Adobe has spent the
past few years filling Photoshop
and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The
November update
cited by the
NYT
’s email adds several new AI features, including
Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view
, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the
Times
, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year,
the
Times
said
that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

NYT

NYT
spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to
The Verge
, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the
NYT
is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to
The Verge

Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of
demand on the network
. Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an
estimated 450% more network traffic
than the same tasks done by human workers.
As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a
recent study
.
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT
This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.
Key findings from the report include:
AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads.
Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.
AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises.
Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.
AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways.
The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.
Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease.
A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.
NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations.
Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.
Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises.
Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

articles.title: On the Importance of Hidden-State Refinement in Masked Diffusion Language Models
articles.summary: Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising masked or corrupted token sequences, allowing token predictions to condition on bidirectional context and update multiple positions in parallel. While each denoising step produces a rich layer-wise hidden-state trajectory, prior work typically focuses only on token-level information and discards these continuous hidden states, leaving their refinement dynamics underexplored. In this work, we analyze hidden-state dynamics in MDLMs and find clear evidence of layer-wise and cross-step refinement: smooth evolution across adjacent layers, greater predictive power in deeper layers, gradual degradation under transformer block removal, and strong final-state alignment across consecutive denoising steps. Motivated by these observations, we propose Cross-Step Recurrent Refinement (CSRR), a mechanism that carries hidden-state information across denoising steps to enhance generation. Extensive experiments show that CSRR improves text generation quality, highlighting the critical role of continuous hidden-state refinement in MDLMs. Project page: https://zhongzero.github.io/Recurrent-DLLM/

articles.title: Within-task hazards of AI agents: unidentified by time-horizon curves, identified by repeated runs
articles.summary: The time horizon of an AI agent is read off a curve: the probability that the agent completes a task, plotted against the time a human needs for it. Several recent analyses fit survival models to this curve and conclude that agents' hazard of failure declines as a task goes on. The curve cannot support that conclusion. Every log-logistic horizon curve with slope $β\le1$ is a mixture of constant-hazard curves, and in a proportional-hazards frailty model the same curve is produced by every within-task Weibull shape $k\geβ$. If runs of a task are conditionally independent, repeated runs restore identification within this model: the probability that two runs both succeed is the single-run curve shifted by $1/k$ on the $\log_2$ time axis. Without the Weibull form, the horizontal distance between these two curves still bears on the direction of the hazard: if the average within-task hazard is non-increasing, the distance is at least one, and so is the population limit of a two-step estimator when the cross-section is log-logistic. We decompose the bias of that estimator into a violation of the shift and a first-step misspecification term, and examine five mechanisms that can break the shift. On METR's public run-level data, under stated assumptions that the data cannot verify, no model's 95% interval for $1/k$ lies entirely above one, and for the five frontier models in the TH1.0 release every interval from runs in different batches lies below one. Under the same assumptions, taken interval by interval and given a log-logistic cross-section, these intervals reject a non-increasing average hazard for the five models, whereas in TH1.1 the result depends on how human times were obtained. Whether $k>1$ reflects a hazard that rises within a task or tasks whose difficulty human time measures only loosely needs experiments that observe the same task at several lengths.

articles.summary: Fluorescence microscopy drives much of modern life science, but accessible imaging setups often yield images degraded by out-of-focus light, limited resolution, and strong signal-dependent noise. Guided conditional flow matching has recently shown strong results for microscopy dehazing and computational super-resolution by learning distributions of plausible restorations. articles.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
articles.summary: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

articles.title: A Framework for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification under Dataset Shift
articles.summary: Graph node quantification is the supervised learning task of estimating the prevalence of different classes within an arbitrary sample of unlabelled nodes from a graph, subject to some form of dataset shift. Existing approaches to graph node quantification typically follow the standard aggregative paradigm, i.e., they use labelled nodes from the graph to train an intermediate node classifier, and obtain an estimated class distribution for the sample by aggregating the classifier's predictions for the individual nodes and then correcting the result via some adjustment strategy that accounts for dataset shift. In this work we propose a framework for graph node quantification that does away with both node-level supervision, since its training phase only requires node samples labelled by their class distribution, and node-level predictions, since it estimates class prevalence values directly, without the need of any intermediate node classifier. The framework thus allows symmetric quantification, since (unlike in standard ``asymmetric'' quantification methods) the labelled items used for training and the unlabelled items on which predictions must be issued are of the same type (i.e., node samples). This framework (that we dub GSQ, for Graph Node Symmetric Quantification) allows building pipelines consisting of a node encoder, an embedding pooler, a prevalence predictor, and an optional post-hoc scaling step. These components can be instantiated by choosing from different trainable and reservoir-based encoders, different pooling operators, and different prediction objectives. We evaluate the GSQ framework on binary and multi-class datasets with different levels of homophily, under prior probability shift and under structural covariate shift.

articles.title: Optimal Transport Meets t-SNE: Integrated Visualization without Batch Effects in OT-tSNE
articles.summary: Visual exploration is an integral step in understanding the structure of datasets. However, systematic variation between datasets collected under different conditions, known as batch effects, can obscure shared structure and complicate their joint visualization. Existing methods often rely on cross-batch nearest-neighbor relations to integrate the batches. Yet, these local correspondences can be unreliable for challenging cross-batch geometries. We propose optimal-transport t-SNE (OT-tSNE), which replaces nearest-neighbor-based matching with globally coupled affinities derived from entropic optimal transport. Controlled synthetic experiments demonstrated that nearest-neighbor-based methods can deteriorate, while optimal-transport affinities and OT-tSNE embeddings remain robust. Across seven real single-cell datasets, we benchmarked OT-tSNE against a broad range of integration and visualization methods and found that it achieves a Pareto-efficient trade-off between batch mixing and biological conservation, and integrates batches particularly well.

articles.title: Verify then Steer: Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery for Continuous Vision-and-Language Navigation
articles.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow language instructions to reach a target in an unseen 3D environment. However, existing methods still struggle to recover from route deviations at test time. We investigate this limitation through the lens of instruction progress, and trace it to a phenomenon we term progress hallucination: agents misinterpret off-route observations as evidence of task progress, causing their internal instruction progress to advance beyond the actual task stage and hindering recovery based on earlier sub-instructions. To address this failure mode, we propose PHAR (Progress Hallucination-Aware Recovery), a test-time recovery framework following a verify-then-steer paradigm. The verifier examines residual-stream representations of the Vision-Language Model (VLM) to identify mismatch of cross-modal evidence along the trajectories, and uses split conformal calibration to control false alarms. When an alarm is raised, the steering module uses a contextual bandit to adaptively select the rewind extent of instruction progress for online recovery. Through extensive experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, our framework enhances the reliability of multiple state-of-the-art vision-language navigation methods at test time.

articles.title: Not All Pairs Align: Caption-Guided Audio-Visual Contrastive Learning
articles.summary: We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

> Abstract:We address the problem of learning audio-visual representations from co-occurring modalities. Multimodal contrastive learning typically assumes that paired observations provide shared views of the same underlying information. While this may be true for datasets collected in constrained environments, it does not always hold. For instance, co-occurring audio and visual signals can differ substantially in their content due to off-screen sounds. Nevertheless, standard contrastive objectives treat all paired samples as equally aligned. In this work, we propose Caption Guided Alignment Aware Loss (CGAAL), a model-agnostic objective that leverages modality-specific captions to estimate semantic agreement between audio and video. CGAAL uses these agreement scores to weight the contribution of each positive pair. A warm-up period and gradual thresholding strategy progressively introduce this alignment-aware training signal. We demonstrate the generality of CGAAL by applying it to three contrastive baselines, consistently improving their performance on audio-visual retrieval.

articles.title: Fractal Neural Synthesis: Constant-Storage Procedural Weight Derivation via Complex Quadratic Boundary Dynamics
articles.summary: Conventional neural networks store synaptic parameters as explicit tensors whose persistent Flash footprint scales linearly (O(W)) with parameter count, constraining resource-limited edge microcontrollers. We formulate and systematically evaluate Fractal Neural Synthesis (FNS), a procedural weight derivation architecture that replaces hidden-layer matrices with a constant 24-byte coordinate seed Theta = (c_x, c_y, ell) in F_64^3 anchored near the complex quadratic bifurcation boundary dM of f_c(z) = z^2 + c. We introduce a large-bailout (R = 256) smooth escape kernel, four zero-overhead geometric sampling apertures--Cartesian Grid, coprime 3x3 Rule-of-Thirds (Z/9Z), phi-Vogel spiral, and multi-scale Harmonic Tripod--and prove conditional Kolmogorov (K_Kolm <= 192 + c_0 bits) and Shannon entropy bounds. articles.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
articles.summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.

articles.title: Evolve to Learn: Gradient-aligned experience evolution for model self-improvement
articles.summary: Self-evolving language models can continuously acquire useful experience through test-time interaction, reflection, and prompt optimization, yet turning such experience into model itself to ensure self improvement remains challenging. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) provides a natural mechanism for internalizing test-time information into model parameters, yet it largely assumes that the gener- ated experience is worth learning. We show that this assumption does not always hold: experiences that improve test-time performance may provide limited or even harmful training signals. To better characterize which experience should be inter- nalized, we systematically analyze diverse mutated experiences across multiple tasks and reflection models, and find that gradient-based alignment is a more reli- able indicator of downstream distillation gains than immediate test-time improve- ment. Based on this finding, we propose E2L, a self-evolution framework that iteratively generates, evaluates, and distills experiences according to their esti- mated training utility. E2L closes the loop between experience generation and parameter learning, enabling agents to autonomously produce experience suitable for self-improvement.

articles.title: Can AI Design a Better nnU-Net? A Hypothesis-Driven Architecture Discovery Loop from Failures to Design Rules
articles.summary: Neural architecture search and LLM-driven evolution often reduce evaluation to a scalar fitness score, discarding failures that could explain why designs succeed or fail. We present a hypothesis-driven architecture discovery loop in which LLM agents diagnose structured error patterns, formulate falsifiable hypotheses, test counterfactual controls under a frozen nnU-Net pipeline, and distill validated mechanisms into executable trigger-to-action rules. Across eight search waves, the loop identifies two principles for 3D medical image segmentation. First, reallocating computation from high-resolution decoders to the mid-encoder preserves thin-anatomy boundaries while reducing cost. Second, support-confined region contrast addresses errors between nested anatomical compartments, with anatomy-dependent triggers selecting when the rule applies. These principles produce LeanNeXt (0.78 MACs and 0.92 training-step time relative to nnU-Net; +1.63 Dice points on four-fold KiTS23 cross-validation) and trigger-routed LeanNeXt+. The latter improves all 15 evaluated CT/MRI settings over nnU-Net and exceeds the 3.3 larger ResEnc-M on 12 of 15 benchmarks at 0.30 its parameter count. Relative to random sampling, one-shot LLM generation, and score-selected agent search, the loop shows how failure analysis can yield reusable design rules across modalities.

articles.title: Does Research-Paper Context Improve LLM-Generated Quadruped Navigation? An Exploratory Simulation Study
articles.summary: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.

articles.title: The Activity Geometry of Discrete Generative Sampling
articles.summary: Iterative refinement is a key capability of diffusion-based generation and has motivated growing efforts to bring similar behavior to discrete diffusion and flow models. A growing line of work enables such refinement by allowing previously generated tokens to be revised during sampling, thereby shaping the coupling between successive sampling states. Despite its growing role in sampler design, this coupling freedom remains insufficiently characterized. We introduce Activity Geometry to study these finite-step couplings through expected transition cost, which we call activity. We show that activity decomposes into the minimum required by the induced marginal transport and an excess term arising from the coupling. Using this minimum as a reference, we propose Minimal-Activity Finite-Time Coupling (MAFTC) to realize prescribed marginals with minimum activity without retraining or additional model evaluations. In the continuous-time limit, the minimum activity per unit time converges to the minimum expected jump rate compatible with the prescribed path. For metric-induced Gibbs paths, we further show that the activity of the kinetic-optimal flux admits a geometric decomposition. We find that total activity alone can obscure coupling excess: a sampler may approach the minimum activity required by the prescribed marginal transport while still retaining substantial coupling excess. In language generation, as the number of model evaluations increases, refinement-based samplers accumulate additional trajectory activity with limited diversity gains, whereas MAFTC reduces trajectory activity while maintaining comparable generation quality and higher lexical diversity.

articles.title: Validating Multi-Model AI-Generated Acceptance Criteria in Requirements Engineering
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering to generate artifacts such as requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, documentation, and code. Their use in requirements engineering raises important questions about correctness, traceability, and hallucination, especially because flawed specifications can affect later design, implementation, and verification activities. While much recent work on AI-assisted software engineering has focused on code generation and code-level validation, the validation of AI-generated specifications has received less attention. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a validation-oriented approach for AI-generated acceptance criteria. The approach combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), multi-model generation, and an explicitly structured human-in-the-loop workflow. We describe a working prototype that allows users to prepare or enter user stories, generate acceptance criteria using several LLMs, optionally augment generation with retrieved requirements-related examples, compare outputs side by side, inspect retrieved context, and select, edit, or regenerate candidate criteria before explicitly submitting a reviewer-finalized version. The system also records model outputs, user interventions, retrieval settings, and final criteria as part of a logged decision process. Rather than claiming that generation accuracy is already improved, the contribution of this work is to operationalize validation as an explicit, inspectable, and accountable process for AI-generated requirements artifacts.

articles.summary: Transit-network design requires evaluating many candidates, but detailed accessibility calculations are too slow to repeat inside an optimization loop. We therefore train a neural surrogate to approximate them. Given a candidate bus network and fixed information about rail service and nearby opportunities, it predicts the calculated spatial change in accessibility. We compare its predictions with routing-derived targets in geographically held-out regions and test specified qualitative relations under controlled input changes. Reference calculations on constructed networks assess the applicability of relations that have a routing-level counterpart. Models with positive predictive skill can still fail basic connectivity tests. One targeted intervention substantially increases pass rates for two connectivity relations while predictive skill also improves. Average prediction error is therefore insufficient when a learned model becomes an optimization objective. Predictive agreement and controlled behavioral tests should be reported separately.

articles.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
articles.summary: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

articles.title: A Description-Derived Drug-Drug Interaction Benchmark Reveals Split-Dependent Molecular Representation Rankings
articles.summary: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is clinically important and poses a distinct challenge for molecular representation learning. Unlike single-molecule property prediction, DDI requires a predictor to compose two molecular representations into a relational outcome. DrugBank provides curator-authored DDI descriptions rather than ready-made categorical labels, so a categorical prediction target must first be derived from the text. We construct a dataset of DDI pairs by mapping processed descriptions to six text-derived categories and define a benchmark with four holdout regimes that restrict train-test chemical overlap from random pairs to scaffold-disjoint evaluation. We then use this benchmark to compare molecular fingerprints, pretrained sequence representations, and graph-derived features across five seeds and multiple classifier heads. Molecular fingerprints lead the high- overlap random split, whereas graph-derived representations lead the drug- and scaffold-holdout regimes, with the gap increasing as molecular overlap is restricted. Changing the classifier head affects absolute performance but not the relative representation ranking. These results show that representation rankings change with test-set novelty under a fixed description-derived label space.

articles.title: The Control-Flow Tax: Specialized Decision Routing for LLM Agent Workflows
articles.summary: An agent can spend almost as much deciding what to do as doing it. In our documentation workflow, control-flow routing accounts for 42.5% of baseline reference cost on the initial task. Lower token prices alone do not solve this control-flow tax: inexpensive general-purpose routers can trigger additional calls to the expensive generator. We evaluate a heterogeneous architecture in which Jev, a specialized System 1 decision model, controls finite actions while Sol generates documents. Across four software tasks, 480 valid runs comprise 470 completions and ten request-limit endpoints. Jev full routing achieves the lowest mean cost and elapsed time on every task, completing all 40 specialist-controlled runs along the shortest trajectory. On the initial task, mean cost falls by 49.6% (95% paired-bootstrap interval: 42.9% to 56.3%) and elapsed time by 33.2% (19.6% to 46.7%). Across three further tasks, cost reductions are 40.5% to 42.9% and concurrent elapsed-time reductions are 12.9% to 14.4%. Existence-only specialization saves just 1.8% on the initial task. Separately, Sol and Jev each select accepted actions on 100/100 reviewed retail states, with Jev using 97.88% less reference cost and 72.30% less mean request time. The results identify two requirements for efficient agent control: inexpensive decisions and trajectories that preserve those savings.

articles.title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you
articles.content:
Title: LLM agents work for their parent companies, not for you

URL Source: https://michaelharley.net/posts/2026/11/01/llm-agents-work-for-their-parent-companies-not-for-you/

Published Time: 2026-11-01T08:02:00.000-05:00

Markdown Content:
In the evenings after work, I will often sit out back on the porch and do some phone rotting. That usually takes the form of me just flipping through reels on Instagram, allowing the algorithm to take me where it may. I usually pair this with a healthy tumbler of rum or bourbon. I'm turning my brain off after work, and I'm just having a good time on the internet. The kids might call it dopamine maxxing? Hell, I don't know. Who gives a shit about what those assholes would call it?

Anywho, I often encounter songs I really really like, and I would like to listen and discover more of please. Instagram makes it hard for me to connect with the band outside of their platform. I was trying to make this connection manually myself at first. I would just email myself a reel from my phone. Then when I'm back on the sofa and in the mood to track down new music, I'd open the reels and do my best to search on Bandcamp or YouTube or try to figure out if some of these musicians had a way to buy music from them. Very few do these days. They send you their Spotify link or send you to their TikTok page. I don't want to do any of that. I'd like to trade US dollars in exchange for some music files I can download onto my computer, where I can listen as much as I like on any device I own thank you please. Retro maxxing.

So, I used Claude Code to build a skill that does this for me. It opens the Instagram reel and attempts to identify the artist and song. It then tries to determine if the artists have a Bandcamp page so I can purchase the songs I want, and if it finds one, it gives me the URL so I can click it to complete the trade I want. I want to buy music from artists who make music I like. That's a fair and wholesome endeavor, I feel, but this recently stopped working.

It turns out Bandcamp added a challenge on their search API page. Ah bummer. No worries, that was an unpublished workaround anyway. As I was mulling over this discovery, the robot went on to explain that it would not help me work around the challenge. _cue Nick Young question marks_

Well, that led me down a whole nother rabbit hole, which is turning into this post. There's another branch of my skill that attempts to locate the same song from the Instagram reel on YouTube, and it'll download the song to my computer if I ask.

So let me get this straight. The robot, which is my robot that I pay a pretty penny for, will not attempt to work around the challenge at Bandcamp so that I can more easily connect with bands to complete a sale, **but it will download the YouTube song, which doesn't send any money to the band or anyone**???

This is the real danger of the frontier AI models. Not that it won't help me hack Bandcamp[[1]](https://michaelharley.net/posts/2026/11/01/llm-agents-work-for-their-parent-companies-not-for-you/#fn1 "And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this."), but that this model doesn't really work for us. Well, they do, but only insofar as Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever else allows them to. In this case, Anthropic is trying to ensure that people can't use their models for evil. I'm not trying to do evil. I'm actually trying to do good! I want to buy something from a small artist on the internet. That's basically the most wholesome thing a person can do on the internet!

Have no doubt, dear reader, these companies want to dominate. They want to capture the market. They want all the money. It'll be the same march to enshittification that happened with Google. A bunch of nerds who built something cool sold out, and it turned into just another business that decided to remove its _don't be evil_ mantra.

Right now, I think the robots are providing real information to the best of their ability, but I think it's only a matter of time until we must wonder if the answers they're providing are real answers that the robot found, or if they're weighted answers Anthropic put there because a company gave it enough money for product placement. I want to know the best robot vacuum according to old reddit or other trusted sources like Wirecutter, weighed and measured according to what I, and thus my robot agent, think are important requirements. I don't want to know which robot vacuum parent multinational conglomerate has a large ad budget.

And it's not just ads. If Anthropic can tell its model not to work around a challenge, then it can tell its model to do whatever the US government tells it to do, including not helping people download copyrighted music. It does that some now, but it's easy to slip the noose on that. For now.

This is the reason I want a local model that runs in my homelab. My robot should work for _me_ and have _my_ best interests in mind, not the interests of US corporate copyright holders. I plan to study up on what "open models" even means. I've been thinking about these as the FOSS version of LLMs, but I think that doesn't exactly map, as the biggest piece seems to be how the model was trained. The Chinese models are likely to refuse to answer questions about Taiwan, for example.

On the _existential threat or tool_ question, I'm firmly in the _tool_ camp, and I really do not like artificial restrictions on my tools. I will do everything I reasonably can to remove those restrictions.

* * *

1.   And to be clear, I'm not trying to work around Bandcamp's challenge. I'm responding to the fact that Claude preemptively told me it wouldn't help me do this. [↩︎](https://michaelharley.net/posts/2026/11/01/llm-agents-work-for-their-parent-companies-not-for-you/#fnref1)

articles.content:
Title: Introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B: Powering Agentic Coding and Private Knowledge Work

URL Source: https://prismml.com/news/bonsai-2-5-27b

Published Time: 2026-11-24

Markdown Content:
Today, we’re introducing Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding, multi-turn tool use, and multi-step task execution. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, it retains the previous release’s 5.9 GB model footprint while significantly improving the capabilities developers need to build agents that work with private files and tools on-device. The result is by far the strongest AI model of its memory footprint for agentic workloads.

With [Ternary Bonsai 2 27B](https://prismml.com/news/bonsai-2-27b), we brought stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool use to local devices. Since then, we’ve focused on making the model more effective across long sequences of tool calls: interpreting results, adjusting when a step fails, and maintaining the task’s objective through the whole interaction. This release also continues our work to make Bonsai more practical by addressing excessive thinking and repetitive loops in the previous model. Compared with Ternary Bonsai 2, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 completes tasks in fewer turns, uses fewer tokens, and delivers results faster and more accurately.

Agentic workflows are particularly sensitive to model degradation: small errors can compound across successive tool calls and derail an entire task. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 significantly narrows the performance gap to the full-precision base model while retaining its compact footprint. Preserving this behavior through longer tasks is an important milestone in improving the intelligence density of models.

We evaluated Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B against both Ternary Bonsai 2 27B and the full-precision Qwen 3.8 27B base model, as reported in the full [whitepaper](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo/blob/main/bonsai-2-5-27b-whitepaper.pdf). We see marked improvements in agentic execution, coding, and multi-turn tool use, as shown in the table below.

| Benchmark | Qwen3.8 27B | Bonsai 2 27B | Bonsai 2.5 27B |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SWE-bench Verified | 80.6 | 60.8 | 75.6 |
| DeepSWE v1.1 (mini-swe-agent) | 30.1 | 0 | 27 |
| Terminal-Bench 2.1 | 70.8 | 52.8 | 60.1 |
| AppWorld | 93.2 | 51.2 | 90.5 |
| τ³-Bench | 72.8 | 69.1 | 73.9 |
| BigCodeBench | 61.5 | 57.2 | 60.3 |
| LiveCodeBench v6 | 87.6 | 83.8 | 83.0 |

On a single NVIDIA H100, Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieves a generation speed of 291 tokens/s with MTP and processes a 2,000-token prompt at 3,200 tokens/s. Even on a consumer-grade RTX 4090, it delivers 204 tokens/s with MTP and a prompt processing speed of approximately 3,060 tokens/s. The demos below follow complete local workflows, from the initial request through intermediate decisions to the final result.

> Demo I: Reproducing and fixing a pytest regression with Bonsai 2.5 27B

For products, this creates room to build assistance directly into the applications where work already happens: a coding assistant working through issues in a private repository, a document application that prepares reviewable summaries, or a desktop assistant that handles recurring analysis. Local deployment lets those products process sensitive material on the user’s device. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B strengthens the model capabilities behind that experience while keeping the compact footprint that makes it practical.

## **Platform Coverage**

Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs via llama.cpp and on Apple devices (Mac, iPhone, iPad) via MLX.

Model weights are available today under the Apache 2.0 License.

Full technical details of our compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in our [whitepaper](https://github.com/PrismML-Eng/Bonsai-demo/blob/main/bonsai-2-5-27b-whitepaper.pdf).

## **Work with Us**

We work with teams to tailor Bonsai models to their applications, from post-training on domain-specific data to optimizing inference for target hardware. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, we’d love to explore how Bonsai can help. Reach out at [sales@prismml.com](mailto:sales@prismml.com).

## **Join Us**

Prism ML emerged from a team of Caltech researchers and was founded with support from Khosla Ventures, Cerberus, and Google, with continuing support from Samsung. We've spent years tackling one of the field's hardest problems: compressing neural networks without sacrificing their reasoning ability.

If you want to help build the next generation of state-of-the-art AI, we'd love to hear from you. Check out our [careers](https://prismml.com/careers) page.

articles.content:
Title: An Active Intrusion Campaign Against Check Point Security Management Servers

URL Source: https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign

Markdown Content:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries.

‍

## Campaign Summary

*   GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.

*   We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims.

*   The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing.

*   We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin.

*   The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers.

*   The actor used [Nmap](https://github.com/nmap/nmap), [Chisel](https://github.com/jpillora/chisel), [Impacket](https://github.com/fortra/impacket), [Paramiko](https://github.com/paramiko/paramiko) and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

*   The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: [CVE-2026-61500](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2026-61500) (Rejetto HFS), [CVE-2025-5777](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2025-5777) (Citrix NetScaler), [CVE-2024-21893](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2024-21893) (Ivanti), [CVE-2026-41089](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-41089) (Windows NetLogon), [CVE-2026-16232](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2026-16232)(Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and [CVE-2026-98432](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2026-98432) (Linux IPv4 UAF).

*   Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets.

*   Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing.

*   We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims.

‍

## Observed Attacker Activities

We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through [ExpressVPN](https://viz.greynoise.io/ips?q=metadata.vpn_service:%22EXPRESS_VPN%22) or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).

‍

### HFS Scanning and Exploitation

The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using [CVE-2026-61500](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2026-61500).

**2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC** - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password.

_Example POST to loginSrp1 and response_

_Decoded hfs\_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested_

‍

**2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC** - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed [CVE-2026-61500](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-61500) for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server.

_Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie_

‍

Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits.

**2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC** - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys.

On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th.

‍

### Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop

**2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC** - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations.

_Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server._

‍

_Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine._

The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration.

_Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant_

They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay.

**2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC -** The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets.

The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and [Chisel](https://github.com/jpillora/chisel), and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy.

‍

### Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration

Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims. During our visibility, the actor was actively working towards deepening their intrusion against Victim A, and we later observed bulk actions on 21 other victim Check Point devices.

Between October 20th and 26th, the adversary had one of their Victim A compromised assets download the Chisel program and run it in client mode allowing them to further scan and interact with the Victim A environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for [CVE-2026-16232](https://viz.greynoise.io/cves/CVE-2026-16232) (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point Management Servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix Netscaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers.

The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.

**2026-10-20 13:54:30 UTC** - First use of exploit.py against a Victim A Check Point server.

**_Excerpt from exploit.py_**_- This CVE-2026-16232 script is purportedly an adaptation of the Metasploit module for the same function. This appears to be how the actor was sending commands to the victim Check Point Security Management Servers._

**2026-10-20 14:17:51 UTC** - spray_portal.py used to scan another Check Point server in the Victim A environment.

_Excerpt from spray\_portal.py - note that this contained common/default/weak passwords, and those apparently tailored for the victim._

**2026-10-21 00:34:51 UTC** - The actor could not get the second compromised Check Point device to report back to the hop, so they created and launched pull_<redacted_id>.py to steal the data from the second Check Point server and save it on the first compromised server, which could help exfiltrate the data back to the hop server.

_Excerpt from pull\_<redacted\_id>.py - The actor named this script after their targeted device. The script runs exploit\_socks.py which runs exploit.py for CVE-2026-16232, enabling the actor to harvest data from the second compromised Check Point device through the first, to the hop box. Notice that this steals credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configuration._

‍

**2026-10-21 02:56:38 to 06:34:40 UTC** - The actor runs broad port scanning using curl, telnet, nmap scripts, a domain controller probe and other tools for internal reconnaissance.

**2026-10-21 06:39:24 to 11:28:04****UTC** - The actor uses exploit scripts against multiple target servers in the Victim A environment.

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - sous-labs/songe: A training engine for your local model, using your idle compute

URL Source: https://github.com/sous-labs/songe

Markdown Content:
### A training engine for your local model, using your idle compute.

[Install](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe#-install) • [How it works](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe#-how-it-works) • [Commands](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe#-commands) • [Roadmap](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/blob/main/ROADMAP.md) • [Discord](https://discord.gg/cBEywVkXjY) • [Website](https://souslabs.ai/)

Use your local model as usual through opencode, pi or any OpenAI-compatible tool. While you work, Songe notices what happens after each of the model's actions: the tool result, the error, your next message. When your agent is quiet, it teaches the model to see those coming. A new version is used only if it passes its checks, and nothing ever leaves your machine.

## ✨ Highlights

*   **Learns from how you work.** Your corrections, stated preferences and the tools' errors become lessons for your own model.
*   **Two kinds of Dreams.** A Quick Dream adds your preferences to the model's instructions in minutes; a Deep Dream trains the model itself while you are away.
*   **Safe by default.** A new version is used only if it does better on your own conversations; one click goes back to any earlier version.
*   **Stays out of the way.** Runs only when your agent is quiet, memory is free and the battery is fine, and stops the moment you are back.
*   **Private.** No account, no telemetry, no cloud. Songe never runs your tools.

## 📥 Install

With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) or [pipx](https://pipx.pypa.io/) (Python 3.11 or later):

uv tool install songe        # or: pipx install songe
songe init

No uv or pipx yet? Either installs in one line:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh    # uv (or: brew install uv)
brew install pipx                                  # pipx on macOS (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install pipx)

Both give Songe its own environment in a lasting place, which its background service needs.

macOS with Homebrew:

brew tap sous-labs/tap
brew trust sous-labs/tap     # newer Homebrew asks this once
brew install songe
songe init

`songe init` finds your model server and your agents, shows what it will change, and asks once:

$ songe init

 Models 3 from LM Studio, listed under Songe
 Agent opencode → Songe models · default granite-4.2-3b-MLX-4bit
 Agent pi → Songe models · choose one with /model
 Data ~/Library/Application Support/songe
 Service starts at login
 Learning new conversations · starts when idle
 Replace loaded copy when a better version is ready

Install? (Y/n)

Then pick a Songe model in your agent (opencode lists them as `songe/songe/<name>`), and work as usual.

Plain pip, and what you need
`pip install songe` works inside a virtual environment; outside one, Homebrew's and most Linux distributions' Python refuse it.

You need a model served locally, and an agent:

|  | Supported | Tested end to end |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model servers | LM Studio, vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp, mlx-lm | LM Studio (macOS), vLLM (Linux) |
| Agents | opencode and pi (set up for you); any OpenAI-compatible tool | opencode, pi |
| Training | Apple Silicon (MLX); NVIDIA and AMD (PyTorch) | Apple Silicon, NVIDIA |

Machines without a GPU still serve and record, but do not train. Tried Songe on another setup? Share the result on the [testing board](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/issues/15).

## 🌙 How it works

```
your agent ──► Songe (127.0.0.1:7613) ──► your model server
                   │ records what happened
                   ▼
            when you are away: a Dream
   read lessons ─► practice ─► train ─► check ─► use only if better
```

|  | Quick Dream | Deep Dream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Takes | a few minutes | an hour or more |
| Does | adds the preferences you stated or showed to the model's instructions | writes practice from your lessons and trains a small adapter on it |
| You see | each new preference, with a before/after where the answer changes | why the new version was or was not used |
| Undo | undo the Quick Dream, or remove one preference | go back to any earlier version |

With **auto-dream** on, Dreams start when your agent has been quiet for a while. Or press **Dream** in the dashboard (`songe open`). A Dream never just disappears: it keeps going on the page, or says why it stopped.

How it learns, in more detail
*   **Reading.** Songe reads each conversation for the moments that teach something: your corrections and stated rules, retries, tool errors.
*   **Practice.** For each lesson your model writes short practice scenes in your agent's own tools. Your real conversations are never trained on.
*   **Training.** The model as it was, shown the lesson, is the teacher; the same model with a small adapter, shown only the scene, is the student (on-policy distillation). Earlier skills are rehearsed so they stay.
*   **Checking.** At the moments you reacted to, the version in use and the new one each answer, and a judge compares what they do. The new version is used only if it does clearly better, does not change what already worked, and its answers stay healthy.

Before the first training Songe measures how much your computer can learn at once, and trains on what fits. See [DESIGN.md](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/blob/main/DESIGN.md).

## ⌨️ Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `songe` | what it is doing |
| `songe status --training [MODEL]` | resolved Deep Dream settings and where they come from |
| `songe open` | the dashboard in your browser |
| `songe models` | each model, and whether it dreams on its own |
| `songe models MODEL on|off` | auto-dream for one model |
| `songe sleep` | start a Deep Dream now |
| `songe undo MODEL` | go back one version |
| `songe pause` / `songe resume` | stop and restart learning |
| `songe doctor` | check the setup |
| `songe forget` | delete recorded conversations (learned versions stay) |
| `songe uninstall` | stop the service and restore your agent settings |

What it changes on your machine
*   Its data folder: `~/Library/Application Support/songe` on macOS, `$XDG_DATA_HOME/songe` on Linux, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\songe` on Windows.
*   A `songe/` folder in LM Studio's models folder with the current learned version. Your own models are never touched.
*   One provider entry in opencode and pi, with a backup.
*   A background service that starts at login.

Upgrade and remove
`uv tool upgrade songe`, `pipx upgrade songe` or `brew upgrade songe`: the service moves to the new version by itself in a quiet moment.

`songe uninstall` stops the service and restores your agent settings; add `--purge` to also delete its data and learned versions. Run it before `brew uninstall songe`.

## 🧭 Roadmap and contributing

Where Songe is going: [ROADMAP.md](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/blob/main/ROADMAP.md). Ideas and bugs are welcome as [issues](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/issues). Questions and results from your nights go in [Discord](https://discord.gg/cBEywVkXjY). To contribute, see [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Security reports: [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/sous-labs/songe/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

articles.title: PenGPT: A Generative Transformer for Handwriting and Sketches
articles.content:
A small transformer that writes and sketches from text. The effort was 80% data, 15% speed and 5% architecture: my first project that follows the Bitter Lesson.
Left.
One phrase in the hands of 21 writers who were held out of training. The model read one to three real words by each of them and carried on in their hand.
Right.
Drawings from typed prompts. I picked these by eye from the best third of the samples; there are unpicked ones further down.
Read the paper
Get the code
Download weights
Last year Zach Wimpee and I trained a tiny GPT to
write cursive
. It worked but it only knew one hand (mine) and it learned from 3,500 words that I wrote on a trackpad.
So here’s the obvious next question: can one small, ordinary transformer learn to hold a pen in lots of hands and draw as well as write? PenGPT is my attempt. There are two models. A 6M-parameter one writes print and cursive and picks up the handwriting of someone it has never seen from a few of their words. A 54M-parameter one draws from a text prompt.
Then I took the thing apart to find out why it works. The answer wasn’t what I expected.
How it works
The whole recipe. Pen points snap to a grid (b) so a word becomes a walk in eight directions plus pen-down and pen-up. Byte-pair encoding merges common runs of moves into tokens (c): this "world" goes from 156 moves to 47 tokens. Everything else is a plain decoder that cross-attends to what it's told.
That’s it for the modality-specific part: ten symbols and a merge count. The same tokenizer handles handwriting and drawings. For handwriting the model is told the text; for drawings it’s told a SigLIP 2 vector so a typed phrase can stand in for a picture.
The data
Almost nobody records pen strokes so I made the handwriting data from scans: 495,590 words by 1,255 writers, mostly from two research collections plus old letters and diaries from public archives. A vision-language model finds legible pages and transcribes them, the pages get cut into words, InkSight traces each word back into strokes and a set of checks throws out bad traces. Between a third and a half of the words survive.
The drawings are 477,670 sketches from ten public datasets. Quick, Draw! has 50 million and I kept the best 0.5%. I’m not releasing the datasets but the paper’s appendix explains how to build them.
Every writer the model knows, saying hello. Each one is placed by its learned vector, with print on the left and cursive on the right. Nobody told the model which was which. Color is the source the pages came from.
Training a model
I compared PenGPT with older approaches then changed one thing at a time and retrained. Here are the rows I found most interesting; the paper has the rest.
