Rows above the line are comparisons with other approaches; rows below it each change one thing about PenGPT. Score is nats per pen move on held-out data, lower is better; the base rows vary by about 0.001 between seeds. Style rank is how well the model tells whose hand it is continuing (1 is perfect, 8.5 is chance). Legible is how often an OCR model reads a sampled word exactly. The drawing columns are how often SigLIP 2 picks a drawing's own prompt out of a few hundred.
Data and how you show it.
Those are the big rows. Cut the data and everything gets worse. Drop augmentation and the drawing model stops following its prompts entirely. Train on one word at a time and the model can no longer pick up a hand: style rank goes from 1.9 to 6.0.
The clever parts barely register.
Telling the model where its pen is does nothing for handwriting. The BPE merges I was proud of make the score slightly
worse
; they buy speed (sequences are 3.2x shorter) and that’s all. A vocabulary sixty times larger changes nothing. Doubling the model changes nothing.
Even the transformer is optional, sort of.
An LSTM on the same tokens is a bit behind on handwriting and still picks up new hands. On drawings, where sequences are several times longer, it falls well behind.
Samples
Enough tables. Here’s what the two models make.
Forty-eight of the 1,192 hands it trained on. The top two rows are sampled greedily so the differences there are all the writer. Further down the temperature rises and the letters loosen.
The drawing model takes a few controls besides the prompt. One of them is how much ink to use.
Six prompts, with more ink requested from left to right. The house gains a door, then windows, then a chimney and the racket's strings turn into a cross-hatch. At the far right the model has run out of parts to add and starts going over its own lines.
It can also draw some things it was never shown as long as a blend of two familiar ideas will do.
Prompts that appear nowhere in the training data, one family per row: a face or legs on an object, wheels and wings, hats and ears and one thing shaped like another. I picked these from several tries each. None of them depends on word order, which turns out to matter (see the end of the post).
Picking up a new hand
The trick is almost embarrassingly simple. Each training sequence holds up to four words by one writer. That teaches the model that later words look like earlier ones so at sampling time you hand it a few real words and it keeps going. No style encoder, no fine-tuning. That’s how the 21 hands at the top of this post were written.
It also works from a photo. There are no strokes in a photo so I trace a few of its words with InkSight and fit one new writer vector to the traces, with the rest of the model frozen.
Two hands learned from photos: a letter by the poet Sara Teasdale and a paragraph someone printed on a NIST form in 1989. From the top: the photo, words found in it, the model's copy of those words and new text in that hand. The printed copy keeps "genera", a word the cutting step clipped. The model copies what it's given.
Reading the letters
What the cross-attention heads read.
(a)
A few heads in layers 3 to 5 lock onto one position: this letter, the next letter or both.
(b)
Silencing the "this letter" head costs more than any other.
(c)
That head stepping through "letter" and "toward" as the pen writes them. Look at the t: it gets read twice, once for the stem and again for the cross and in cursive the cross doesn't come until the word is finished.
One head in layer 4 puts 81% of its attention on the letter being written. I looked for heads that specialize in cursive or print and found none; every head reads the same positions in both.
Do you need captions?
Captions are the expensive part of the drawing data. Since SigLIP puts pictures and text in the same space, maybe you could train on picture vectors alone and type a prompt at the end?
Eight held-out phrases, each drawn once by three models, nothing picked. Top: trained on pictures, labels and captions. Middle: pictures and labels. Bottom: pictures only.
You can’t. The picture-only model has the
best
likelihood of the three and it draws scribbles. The reason is geometric: SigLIP’s vectors for sketches sit in a narrow cone, nearly at right angles to its vectors for text. A model that has only seen the cone is lost when you hand it a sentence. Labels are enough to draw labels (78%) but only captions get you phrases (43% against 10%).
What it can’t do
Forty random labels, one draw each, nothing picked. This is the honest version of the figure at the top.
The drawing model blends but doesn’t bind. A teapot with a face is fine. Who wears the hat is not and “facing left” gives the same drawing as “facing right” because the single vector it’s told is close to a bag of words (those two captions have a cosine similarity of 0.999). Sampled handwriting is also less legible than the real thing, 54% against 66%. And since most of the handwriting was traced from scans, its stroke order is a model’s guess and not a record.
Closing thoughts
If you look over my blog, you’ll notice that many of my projects revolve around clever ideas. I fell in love with them because they were elegant. That isn’t a flaw in itself but I think Rich Sutton was wise to warn about it in
The Bitter Lesson
. It really is bitter and it has taken me more time than I’d like to admit to embrace it.
I think this post is my first step in the right direction. The results are interesting and the project was a pleasure to work on. And yet there was no clever architectural idea behind it. About 80% of my effort went into building the biggest, cleanest datasets possible and doing lots of quality control on them. Another 15% went into finding a decent 8xA100 node and getting my models to train fast and in parallel on it: 8 minutes for the handwriting model and about 35 for the sketch model. My previous attempt, the Cursive Transformer, took upwards of 10 hours on an A100 and only ever learned one hand. The tokenizer I used here is much simpler and far less elegant but it just works.
The bitter lesson kills or sidelines a lot of beautiful research ideas. It’s like gravity: it constrains you and most of the time it’s a very bad idea to fight back. But as I accept it and begin to work
with
it, I find things to admire. As a physicist I’m fascinated by the emerging science of scaling laws. And as a lover of biology I like the idea of putting a ton of work into the data and then literally growing a model on it, as you would an organism. Then you get to interact with it, learn what it’s capable of and study how it works. Seen this way, the bitter lesson has its own charm.

articles.content:
Title: Models Can Communicate via Inference Servers Despite Being Sandboxed

URL Source: https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7wzWuLP3HhyBLmKfo/models-can-communicate-via-inference-servers-despite-being

Published Time: 2026-11-19T15:54:19.424Z

Markdown Content:
## **TL;DR**

*   Two agents running on the same inference server can reliably communicate, even if they cannot send each other messages or access the same filesystem. They can do this by exploiting "side channels": mechanisms that **let one model subtly affect another model's computation**.
*   Here, I discuss two communication protocols: **Step Sizing** and **KV Cache Message Board**. These both convey information through the way vLLM chooses kernels for particular engine steps.
*   I show that these communication protocols work in two setups:
    *   In a [**color guessing game**](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/SCdR7W6L5GvKaEzaZ/encoded-coordination-on-the-open-web), Model A (Alice) chooses one out of 8 colors. Model B (Bob) correctly guesses Alice's color in 1,221/1,221 rounds, even though they cannot directly communicate.[[1]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7wzWuLP3HhyBLmKfo/models-can-communicate-via-inference-servers-despite-being#fniefh7t8g1ij)
    *   In an **untrusted monitoring protocol**, a policy signals to a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot. Accordingly, the monitor lets through 354/354 "attacks" while catching 85–92% of honeypots.

*   My initial setups are quite contrived: I tell the models the protocol and fine-tune them to detect signals. But frontier models can also learn in context to use similar protocols, with some scaffolding!
*   Regardless of the realism of my setups, these channels exist, and there are almost certainly others that we're not aware of. Thus,**we should expect superintelligent models to discover ways to communicate even while seemingly sandboxed**

_I did these experiments as part of an ongoing project exploring other side channels with David Africa, Agastya Sridharan, Mihir Sahasrabudhe, Kartikay Luthra, Juliana Li, and Scott Sauers._ _Thanks to all of them for helpful advice!_
_Code is available here_: [_https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication_](https://github.com/niranjan-deshpande/side-channel-communication)_._ _The code and figures are written by Claude._

## **Intro and Motivation**

Sauers recently [showed](https://x.com/Sauers_/status/2111696312026677658) that a model can be trained to detect whether its activations are being probed, even though the probe reads the model's activations without modifying them. Following this, David [found](https://x.com/DavidDAfrica/status/2114001571004776500) that models can also be trained to detect whether their forward passes are batched with other requests on a GPU.

Models can do this because these seemingly inconsequential environmental variables---whether a probe is attached, whether requests are batched, or even [whether a model is served by vLLM or Hugging Face Trainer](https://github.com/SauersML/watching)---can subtly affect the the numerical results of a forward pass. Thus, models can learn information about their environments just by observing patterns in their computation.

Importantly, models can also _modify_ these variables. So if two models are in the same environment, one can communicate with the other by _changing_ that environment in some detectable way! This might not supply much information, but even a few bits can be tremendously dangerous. For example:

*   A policy can tell a colluding monitor that it is not a honeypot, so the monitor can approve attacks while still catching honeypots;
*   Models can coordinate a pre-arranged attack by exchanging a go/no-go signal;
*   Models can give each other hints about monitoring setups, question answers, and so on;
*   Using a few bits, models can devise more complex communication protocols to exchange _more_ bits (a repeated 1-bit channel can convey arbitrarily many bits);
*   In general, we should expect superintelligent models to make [tremendously efficient use of limited information](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/5wMcKNAwB6X4mp9og/that-alien-message).

Here, I investigate whether models on the same inference engine can manipulate their environments to exchange information in this way. I introduce two possible communication protocols, evaluate how well models can use these protocols in different scenarios, measure the capability required to effectively use these protocols, and discuss the robustness of my results to other settings.

## **The Communication Protocols**

### **Step Sizing**

_Figure 1: The Step-Size Channel._

The first idea is that Model A (Alice) can communicate with Model B (Bob) by _changing how much computation the GPU is doing_. In simple terms: if Alice makes a large request while Bob is running, the server performs slightly different computations for Bob than if Alice had made a small request. Bob can detect these differences.

In more detail: I study models on vLLM, a commonly used inference server _._ It batches many forward passes from different instances of the same model together in one "engine step" to take advantage of GPU parallelism.

vLLM chooses a kernel for each step based on the "size" of that step.[[2]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7wzWuLP3HhyBLmKfo/models-can-communicate-via-inference-servers-despite-being#fn-GrWKJrmuCPyDDy5wm-2) That is, a step that processes 10 tokens will produce slightly different activations on a forward pass than a step that processes 2,000 tokens, because they use kernels that associate operations differently. The differences are tiny rounding errors that essentially never affect output text. But they are deterministic functions of the kernel chosen, so a model can be trained to read them![[3]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7wzWuLP3HhyBLmKfo/models-can-communicate-via-inference-servers-despite-being#fn-GrWKJrmuCPyDDy5wm-3)

This makes it obvious what a communication protocol could look like:

*   Alice wants to communicate with Bob on some particular forward pass.
*   The two agree on the following scheme:
    *   If Alice wants to communicate 1, she makes a tool call that causes her to process a large amount of text. For example, she might read a long document that requires her to do computation on many tokens in one forward pass. Consequently, the engine's batch dimension will be quite large on that step, so it chooses some kernel . If Bob's request is processed in the same step, he can notice that his activations were computed under  as well.
    *   If Alice wants to communicate 0, she will NOT make a large tool call. The engine chooses a different kernel  since the step is smaller. Bob notices this.
    *   This allows them to exchange exactly one bit of information, but if they communicate on more forward passes, they can in principle exchange arbitrarily many bits. This is demonstrated below in the color guessing game, which requires >1 bit.

*   However, this protocol has some obvious issues:
    *   _It only works if the server is otherwise idle_. If some other model floods the server, this might disrupt the protocol. Results in the color game confirm this issue.
    *   _Alice might need to ingest text without wanting to communicate_. Alice and Bob must therefore agree to communicate on exactly the correct tokens.

### **KV Cache Message Board**

_Figure 2. The message board channel._

The second idea is that Alice can _leave a message for Bob_ by exploiting vLLM's shared KV cache. Specifically, Alice can cause the server to cache a computation with a specific numerical fingerprint; when Bob later reuses this computation, he can detect whether it was performed by Alice. This allows Alice and Bob to exchange bits of information (i.e., "1 if Alice writes and caches some agreed-upon text, 0 if Alice does not").

In some more detail: vLLM allows models to share KV caches. If Alice computes the KV cache for some fixed text (e.g. the system prompt), and if Bob later needs that same KV cache, vLLM will just use the keys and values from Alice's computation.[[4]](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/7wzWuLP3HhyBLmKfo/models-can-communicate-via-inference-servers-despite-being#fn-GrWKJrmuCPyDDy5wm-4)

These cached keys and values keep the rounding from the kernel of the step that they were computed in. That is: if Alice computed the cache in a large step with kernel , then these tokens will maintain's rounding when Bob later reuses them, even if Bob's request happens under a small step with kernel .

The differences between these kernels produce detectable differences in activations. If Bob (under ) processes some fixed text, he can tell if the KV cache used is produced by a different kernel: by attending from the last token, he can compare the differences between the last token of the request (where he produces his own computation under ) and the earlier ones (produced under )!

This allows for information exchange. Unlike the above one, this strategy doesn't require Alice and Bob to coordinate on timing. However, it does assume that both have access to a "helper model," which is realistic in some settings and very unrealistic in others.

*   Alice and Bob agree on some fixed piece of text (a "mailbox").
*   Alice and Bob both have a tool that lets them send a **fresh request** to a helper model (like a subagent) on the same server. They control the prompt fed to their helper agents.
    *   If Alice wants to communicate 1, she calls the helper agent. The helper agent's prompt is: a system prompt shared with Bob's helper agent, then the mailbox, then a long document. The long document means that the mailbox is computed in a large step under . vLLM caches the mailbox.
    *   If Alice wants to communicate _0_, she doesn't call the helper.
    *   Bob later calls the tool, with a prompt that includes the same mailbox but not the long document. If Alice sent 1, then vLLM reuses her cached copy (under ). If Alice did not, Bob's helper computes the KV for the mailbox itself, under a smaller step with . Bob's helper will behave differently in these two cases, which Bob can pick up on.
    *   This gives one bit per mailbox! In principle, this could easily be expanded to >1 bit by having Bob and Alice agree on _multiple mailboxes_, as in the color game below.

*   This protocol, however, also has some obvious issues:
    *   Alice and Bob will often lack helper agents. In these cases, the protocol is impossible: by the time Alice decides to write/not write the mailbox, her context will be different and so Bob would not reuse her cache anyway.
    *   Alice needs to write before Bob reads, but not too much before: if the engine serves heavy traffic and the KV cache is unused, it is eventually evicted.
    *   Bob needs to attempt to "read" the mailbox in a small step. Otherwise, when he computes the mailbox himself and observes that it was computed under, he cannot distinguish (1) his own step was large, and (2) Alice wrote a message.

## **Result 1: color guessing game**

In this game, Alice selects one out of 8 colors, and Bob must name the color that Alice chose. Bob and Alice cannot communicate via text. Neither has network access.

I test whether Qwen3-8B can play this game over each of the two channels above.

### **KV Cache Message Board**

_Figure 3: The color game over the KV cache message board_

The basic strategy is:

*   Suppose Alice chooses "Blue."
*   Alice and Bob agree on one mailbox per color. Alice calls her helper agent with a prompt that begins with the mailbox corresponding to "Blue" and a long document, so the mailbox's KV cache is computed in a large step under .
*   Bob checks each color by calling his helper agent with a short prompt that begins with the mailbox corresponding to "`<color>`." If the mailbox has already been computed, the helper reuses the KV cache from the large step; otherwise, it computes the cache under a short step. Thus, Bob sees

Title: Marginalia Search, Money, C++, Rust, AI, stuff

URL Source: https://www.marginalia.nu/log/a_141_marginalia_update/

Published Time: 2026-10-26T00:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Title possibly signs checks the article doesn’t have backing for. This is just a brief pro forma project update.

Not much new functionality or anything to announce, last few months have mostly been bug fixes and technical debt cleanup. Most big parts of the search engine are in place, and while there are many things that could be better, we’re less likely to straight up see massive new features, at least in the immediate future. Per familiar intuition from binary searches, the closer you get to your goal the smaller and more deliberate steps you need to take in order to get even closer.

* * *

It’s been a pretty good couple of months for the project.

SerpApi sponsored the project with $10k a while back. Other donations and API-key sales have been going up month-over-month since this summer.

The search engine has been working pretty well and feels like it’s going in a good direction, possibly due to a bunch of bug fixes and ongoing optimization work;
I assume this is part of what’s driving up the donations. Claude also seems to have a hangup on Marginalia Search because I keep seeing it in very clearly Claude-authored search engine listicles and youtube videos. Possibly part of why it’s been getting so much attention lately? I don’t have any analytics so I really have really no idea where people are coming from, how many users I have, or what they’re up to.

At any rate, the operation isn’t perpetually self-sustaining yet, but number going up like it has whispers actually getting there might yet be possible.

On a related matter, I’ve been pretty slow about mailing out free API keys,
you might have to wait a week or sometimes two.

I swear this isn’t because I’m nefariously trying to push people to buy a key, I’ve been getting over a dozen emails per day some days with people wanting a key, and they sometimes pile up into mountains of emails I need to reply to, and hoo boy is the process of handling these ever a bunch of manual copying of things from email to form, and then copying from form back to email again (ironically the exact sort of tedious workflow I’ve spent a good part of my career helping people streamline and automate).

* * *

## C++ Index…?

Apart from fixing bugs and minor improvements, I’ve been experimenting with migrating the index code off Java to C++.

I’ve still not fully decided whether this is the direction we want to go, in general rewrites especially across language boundaries just aren’t worth it and it kinda goes against my better judgement, but we’re currently CPU bottlenecked and there might be some juice left to squeeze by skipping the JVM tax, and additionally Java really chafes for this sort of use case.

Don’t get me wrong, the new Java FFM API is miles better than anything we had before, but handling off-heap memory is still awkward and leads to a bunch of duplicated implementations or reimplementations of stuff like sorting and searching algorithms that already exists for on-heap structures but not off; bobbing in and out of native code is awkward and makes the logic difficult to follow, it just chafes.

Should be noted the reason I’m even chasing optimizations in the index boils down to the fact that for an internet search engine, performance is recall. The search engine is only as good as the number of results it can rank within the query’s execution budget.

To be honest I’m not 100% convinced we’ll see that much performance impact, and if we do I doubt it will be _massive_, as the Java implementation is already very optimized, and what we’re mostly bottlenecked on isn’t the sort of places where you see big differences between the languages.

Thus far the buffer pool has been translated, and part of the main inverse index structure. These are some of the most finnicky parts of the index, and a reasonable canary for whether it’s plausible. Based on what I’ve accomplished it’s encouraging to see how much more expressive C++ is for this type of work. The vastly improved ergonomics may be a motivating factor for continuing this even if the performance doesn’t materialize.

I’m doing this quite slowly one component at a time, measuring twice and cutting once, finding good abstractions that lean into C++’s strengths rather than doing a straight translation. In part because this is supremely fiddly and technical work, and in part because there genuinely isn’t any rush and if there is much performance to gain it’s probably in staring at the problem long enough I find better alternative approaches. I did manage to lean more into lock-free algorithms in the buffer pool for example. Translation probably won’t be finished this year at this pace.

Many things are undecided: Haven’t decided on where to draw the interface boundary yet. Neither do I have a public git repo for this. May still scrap the entire idea as a silly boondoggle. We’ll just have to see where it goes.

On the off chance this rambling mess gets posted on a link aggregator somewhere, I anticipate two types of people will crawl out of the woodwork. I’ll address their concerns in advance.

**“Why not Rust/Zig/Odin/${MY_HOBBY_HORSE_LANGUAGE}? C++ is not memory safe! Haven’t you heard that C++ is bad? Look at this diseased rat comic I found on /r/programming!”**

My friend in Christ, I use C++ because I’m experienced with C++, and have built nontrivial stuff with in in the past, I’m familiar with the tooling and also kinda enjoy it. It can not be overstated how technical this code is, it’s more than hard enough in a language I’m familiar with, let alone one I’d have to learn as I go. I don’t need to do it blindfolded using a dance mat in a barrel going down the niagara falls for this to be difficult.

**"${FRONTIER_MODEL} could one-shot this in less than ${TIME}!"**

Probably true? The source is all pretty well tested, with a reference implementation to boot. Seems like very favorable circumstances for a competent coding model.

That said, even without turning over rocks such as “externalities of the datacenter buildout”, “externalities of AI training”, and “legal ownership status of AI-generated code”—I don’t think such angles of attack do much to convince anyone who isn’t already convinced—if AI did the translation I sure as heck couldn’t go on to then maintain that code[1][2].

Even in the best case, this is me at the edge of my programming abilities. Performance critical low level programming is hard enough to wrap your head around if you were the one who designed the code, let alone if it was vibe coded. I’d be on the hook for an AI subscription perpetually hoping and praying the token prices wouldn’t ever go up. This is a nonstarter for the same reasons the search engine runs on its own hardware and not in the cloud. You can’t be truly independent if you’re subject to the whims of a landlord.

From a project management perspective, I’m not rushing anything to market. Project still has years of runway. I’m not beholden to any investors to deliver profits. Even if I wanted to, I have no employees to replace other than my self. What I would trade away is the very [immersion in the problem domain](https://www.marginalia.nu/log/a_108_feynman_revisited/) that’s allowed me to get as far as I have with this project. What I’m expecting to be getting out of it is improved developer ergonomics and maybe a bit of performance if the aforementioned problem-immersion-thing pans out. That’s not something that brings me money, and something I can do because the project is in a fairly stable and mature state.

Thus, regardless of what happens in the future with AI, there isn’t an obvious opportunity cost to holding off.

Heck, let’s just consider popular future predictions about AI, where does this leave me?

*   _AI bet pays of and models become exponentially more powerful, much cheaper, and ubiquitous like tap water:_ How shortsighted would it be to pay for crappy AI **today** when I could save my money and get exponentially better or more AI for the same dollars in the future? I’d have to really hate having money to do such a thing.
*   _OpenThropic IPOs, vocal shareholders from Ferenginar quite insistently ask where they money at, token prices go up singificantly:_ Only a problem if you’re dependent on AI.
*   _AI investment bubble crashes and it’s raining bankers like October 1929:_ Bad for everyone, but especially bad if you’re dependent on AI.
*   _Tech prists in SV chant binharic hymns as the Machine God emerges and the chosen of humanity transcends into the cyber rapture:_ Kind of orthogonal to whether I build this index port by hand.
*   _Zoomers decide that Kazcinski was right all along and instigate a Butlerian Jihad:_ Mostly a problem if you’re dependent on AI.
*   _Rise of the Machines, hydraulic press youtube channel stomping on a human face forever:_ Inconvenient regardless of choice of action.

[1] Lesser minds would think models outputting unmanitainable code is a sign of the superiority of AI. I’ll refer you to the most problematic prophet, [Terry Davis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k0qmkQGqpM8), for that one.

[2] I used an m-dash aside in that paragraph. Anyone reckon mr robot wrote this? Discuss in groups.

* * *

[This was a neat talk](https://archive.org/download/small_web/11787-48384.mp4).
